posts.caption: In 2021, one engineer typed one wrong command and 3.5 billion people lost the internet in a single instant. Not hacked. Not attacked. Just one wrong line of code during a routine maintenance check. Facebook's own engineers couldn't even log in to fix it, their access tools were on the same servers that just vanished. They had to physically drive to data centers and override servers by hand. One by one. 6 hours. $60 million lost every single hour. And the exact same vulnerability? Still exists right now. The internet is more fragile than you think.

2021 mein ek engineer ne ek galat command type ki aur 3.5 billion logon ka internet ek pal mein band ho gaya. Hack nahi hua. Attack nahi hua. Bas ek routine maintenance check ke dauran ek galat line of code. 6 ghante. Har ghante 60 million dollar ka nuksaan. Internet utna strong nahi jitna hum sochte hain.

There is a sound that only 2% of people can hear. Scientists have studied it for 50 years and still have no answer. It's called The Hum — and the leading theory is that it's the Earth itself vibrating at a frequency most humans aren't built to detect. A woman heard it for 11 years, moved across the country to escape it, and it followed her to the new house. Stop right now, close your eyes, and listen. What do you hear?

We call space the final frontier. But we've barely explored our own planet. Earth is stranger than anything we've found out there — and most people have no idea. From perfect solar eclipses to oceans deeper than mountains are tall, this is the planet you thought you knew.

In 1974, a man calculated the exact day he would die and spent a year preparing for it. What happened next is stranger than the prediction itself. Frank was obsessed with numerology. He told his family, quit his job, and gave away everything he owned. When the day came and went without incident, he thought he'd beaten fate. He hadn't.

In Renaissance Europe, science was being transformed into a practice anyone could participate in and even enjoy. The field of astronomy grew rapidly as new instruments were crafted to make discoveries, as you can see on the August page of our 12,026 Human Era calendar. That is when champions like Tycho Brahe, an eccentric man with a metal nose, achieved notoriety by throwing astronomy parties and collecting great volumes of star data that we still use today.

@1x.technologies just unveiled its next-generation robotic hand for NEO, its humanoid robot.
 
We’re talking 24 degrees of freedom, human-like dexterity, tactile sensing, and enough strength to handle real everyday tasks.
 
It can pick up coins, use tools, zip up a jacket, pour tea, plug in a USB-C charger, wipe down surfaces, and even wash its own hands.
 
The impressive part isn’t that it looks human.
 
It’s that it can feel, adapt, and safely interact with the real world around it.

This is Dario Cecchini, one of Tuscany’s most famous butchers, a true icon of Italian food culture. 🥩⁠
At his restaurant in Panzano in Chianti, meat is prepared over open flames and served in a communal dining experience where strangers become friends around the table.⁠
⁠
It's more than just a meal, a celebration of Tuscan traditions, hospitality, and the joy of sharing food together.⁠
🎥: @rororosiex_

This unusual structure in China is known as the “Shadowless Church,” but it was never designed as a traditional church.⁠
⁠
Created by Shanghai Dachuan Architects in 2019, the 65-square-meter art installation is made from thousands of white aluminum tubes arranged around a light steel frame. The open design allows sunlight to pass through almost every part of the structure, giving it its unusual appearance.⁠
⁠
The installation was inspired by the light of Provence and sits among lavender fields a

Beneath the surface of a glacier to reveal a hidden world carved entirely by nature. ❄️💙⁠
During summer, meltwater cuts intricate tunnels and channels through the ice, creating remarkable hydraulic systems hidden beneath the glacier.⁠
⁠
An adventurous spirit is all it takes to discover these breathtaking formations and witness the power of nature at work.⁠
⁠
🎥: @sheepmountainair

This road on Siargao Island in the Philippines looks almost like a tunnel made of coconut trees. 🌴⁠
⁠
Known as Coconut Road, this stretch near Maasin runs through one of the island’s many coconut-growing areas.⁠
⁠
For generations, coconut farming has been an important source of income for people across Siargao, with farmers traditionally turning the dried coconut meat, or copra, into a valuable crop.⁠
⁠
Siargao is known for its beaches and surf spots, but places like this are part of what makes

This might be the most charming Uber ride in Lancaster. 🐴⁠
In the heart of Pennsylvania Dutch Country, horse-drawn carriages are still a common sight, offering a glimpse into a slower and more traditional way of life.⁠
⁠
From a regular ride to a horse and carriage, this is transportation with a touch of nostalgia. ⁠
How beautiful is that? 🤎⁠
🎥: @_risany_

@joe_masini experienced true Italian hospitality firsthand. ⁠
A warm welcome, local kindness, and thoughtful gestures are what turn a simple Airbnb stay into an unforgettable memory.⁠
⁠
Can you think of a better way to arrive at your accommodation?

People actually live on these narrow strips of land in the Netherlands, with water on both sides of their homes.⁠
⁠
The unusual landscape of the Loosdrecht Lakes dates back centuries, when peat was dug from the wetlands and used as fuel. The long strips between the trenches were left behind as the peat dried, while the excavated areas slowly filled with water and became the lakes we see today.⁠
⁠
Some of these narrow strips survived, and homes were later built along them. Today, the area is know

Did you know that some of the most famous fruit sorbets in Paris are served inside their original fruit shells and peels?⁠
⁠
Made with fresh fruit pulp and water, these colorful desserts keep the natural shape and flavor of the fruit, creating a simple yet unforgettable treat.⁠
⁠
How hungry did this make you? 🤤⁠
🎥: @jacksdiningroom

Nature has a way of tricking the eye.⁠
⁠
At first glance, some places don’t even look real. Light, minerals, weather, and time all come together to create scenes that feel more like illusions than real landscapes.⁠
⁠
But nothing here is edited. It’s just nature doing what it does best in the most unexpected way.⁠
⁠
By: Shelter, @1ishome zensunni_wanderers @cedricletsch

@roosmarijn.malmberg showed us a rare glimpse into the fascinating world of a conch. 🐚 ⁠
⁠
Fun fact: conchs are actually giant sea snails, and that incredible spiral shell can take several years to fully grow. ⁠
⁠
This is a unique look at one of the ocean’s most interesting creatures! ⁠
⁠
Have you ever tasted conch before?

This tiny frog looks almost too delicate to be real. 🐸⁠
⁠
Glass frogs get their name from their translucent skin, which can make parts of their bodies, including their internal organs, visible from below.⁠
⁠
Found in the forests of Central and South America, these remarkable frogs are usually small, green, and spend much of their time high in the trees.⁠
But when you look underneath one, you can see exactly why they earned the name “glass frog.”⁠
⁠
By: @tomas_malco_malik @zmachacek6710 @el_mont

In Kisumu, Kenya, thousands of people are working together to change the way HIV prevention is viewed. By making medical care more accessible and challenging the stigma around PrEP, advocates are not only helping to save lives but also empowering women at increased risk to take control of their health. Join National Geographic Explorer and photographer @renaeffendiphoto who traveled to the city to see their impact firsthand. 

Learn more about HIV prevention in Kenya at the link in bio. | @gilea

While living in a fishing village on Mexico’s Baja California peninsula, photographer @nicolas.hahn noticed that the midday winds pushed all kinds of sea creatures close to shore. During one snorkeling session, he discovered this remarkable scene: a collection of mauve stingers, a type of small bioluminescent jellyfish. Hahn got stung a few times around his mask, but the pain was worth it as his underwater lens captured every last tentacle in astonishing detail.

Filming wildlife in the rainforest canopy after dark is no easy feat, especially when the animals are small, elusive, and on the move. But from platforms high in the trees, researchers are using thermal binoculars to capture extended, close-up footage of certain nocturnal species in the rainforests of Panama and Peru.

Discover what scientists are finding in the rainforest canopy after dark at the link in bio. 

Video by Trevor and Lucy Hughes

Witness the rise of a king. 🦁

Coiled around a tree branch in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, this highly venomous bush viper (Atheris mongoensis) was photographed by National Geographic Explorer @thomas.nicolon. Though more than 30,000 people in sub-Saharan Africa die from venomous snakebites each year, it is believed that the number may be double due to unrecorded deaths.

See more Photos of the Day at the link in bio.

When it comes to weight management, we usually think about diet and exercise, but researchers are finding that sleep may play a bigger role than many people realize. With nearly 35 percent of Americans getting less than seven hours of rest a night, experts are trying to understand what prolonged sleep loss could mean for weight over time. 

Learn how sleep can affect your weight at the link in bio. 

Photograph by Rebecca Hale (@beckythale)

Who knew the ocean has a public transport system 🦀
 
Columbus crabs aren’t built for long-distance swimming, so this little crab takes a shortcut through the open ocean. By hitchhiking a ride on a turtle, he find transport, a new home and some unexpected company.

More than meets the eye 👀

Ancient ancestors of the dolphin hid from the sun’s UV rays using two light-detecting spots. Fascinatingly, some inherited mutations that allowed them to perceive light and shade together, so they could visualise their environment - essentially becoming the first proper eyes.

Find out where to watch Evolution via the link in our bio 🔗💚

Treehoppers might be tiny, but they’ve got plenty to say! They communicate through vibrations sent along the plants they live on, most of which are too quiet for us to hear. But when danger appears, sending the right signal can make all the difference.

Dogs move differently to humans. They have a digitigrade posture, which means they walk on their toe bones. This anatomy allows longer and more efficient strides so they run faster and jump further. With less surface area touching the ground, they also move with more agility and greater stealth.
